hints: Look closely at the treatment: $60^{\circ}C$ for 10 minutes on a small section of stem. What does that temperature do to living cells in that section?
Now compare the two tissues: which one depends on living cells and metabolic energy, and which one is made of dead, hollow tubes driven by a purely physical pull?
walkthrough:
**Think about what heating does**

Heating to $60^{\circ}C$ for 10 minutes will kill living cells in that small band of stem. Proteins denature and membranes are destroyed, so any process needing living cells there will stop.

**Apply this to phloem**

Phloem transport needs living sieve tube elements and companion cells. Loading and unloading sucrose uses ATP and living membranes to create pressure gradients. Kill those cells and translocation stops.

**Apply this to xylem**

Xylem vessels are already dead when functional. They are hollow, lignified tubes with no cytoplasm. Water moves up by transpiration pull, cohesion and adhesion, which is a physical process that does not need living stem cells. So xylem sap keeps moving past the heated zone.

options.A: Incorrect. Phloem cannot continue because its living cells are killed by the heat, even though xylem does continue.
options.B: Incorrect and back to front. It is phloem that stops and xylem that continues, not the other way round.
options.C: Correct. Phloem transport stops because living cells are destroyed, while xylem transport continues because dead vessels work by physical transpiration pull.
options.D: Incorrect. Xylem does not stop because it does not rely on living cells in the stem, only phloem stops.
